videos.title_after: Police Took His Phone. Then They Opened It.

snippet_before.title: Police Pulled 127 Days of His Location
snippet_before.description:
A police officer arrests you and takes the phone from your pocket. Can he open it without a warrant?

This episode explains Riley v. California, the 2014 Supreme Court case that changed how the Fourth Amendment applies to the device most people carry everywhere. The Court had to decide whether a phone is just another item in your pocket, or something different in kind: messages, photos, location history, apps, and the private record of a life.

We trace David Riley's traffic stop, the older search-incident-to-arrest rule, the unanimous Supreme Court decision, and why the phrase "get a warrant" became the new baseline for phone searches after arrest.

This is an educational documentary, not legal advice.

Visual note: this video uses AI-generated symbolic reconstructions and motion graphics. They are not authentic footage, and no real-person likeness is intended.

Next episode: the location trail your phone leaves behind.

videos.title_before: They Took Their House Over $40 — and Never Charged Anyone
videos.title_after: Their Son Was Charged. The City Came for His Parents' House.

snippet_before.title: They Took Their House Over $40 — and Never Charged Anyone
snippet_before.description:
Their son sold about $40 of drugs near the family home in Philadelphia. Nobody in the family was charged with a crime — and the city still moved to take the whole house.

This is civil forfeiture. Under it, the government sues the PROPERTY itself — the case is literally captioned against "the house" — so the usual protections that come with being accused of a crime don't apply. In Philadelphia, owners were pushed through "Courtroom 478" with no judge and often no lawyer, while the cash and homes seized helped fund the very prosecutors and police who took them.

Christos and Markela Sourovelis were locked out of their own home. In 2014 the Institute for Justice brought a federal class action; in 2018 the city settled with a consent decree that ended the abusive program and set up a roughly $3 million fund to compensate victims. The family kept their house.

#CivilForfeiture #Philadelphia #Sourovelis #PropertyRights #Law #Documentary

videos.title_before: He Had No Lawyer — So He Beat the Supreme Court
videos.title_after: He Had No Lawyer. So He Wrote the Supreme Court in Pencil.

snippet_before.title: He Had No Lawyer — So He Beat the Supreme Court
snippet_before.description:
He couldn't afford a lawyer, so a Florida court made him defend himself — and convicted him. Then, from a prison cell, Clarence Earl Gideon mailed the U.S. Supreme Court a handwritten letter.

This is Gideon v. Wainwright (1963): how one pauper's petition forced a unanimous Supreme Court to guarantee an appointed lawyer for every poor defendant in America — the promise behind "if you cannot afford a lawyer, one will be appointed for you" — and the underfunded system it left behind.

▶ Watch the full Landmark Rights Cases playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLKcrM3x4g1h9uB4_PDJQNUEX2oNUmAZZ9

⏱ Chapters
0:00 The prisoner who beat the Court
0:39 The right that's younger than you think
1:35 On trial with no lawyer
3:24 The letter — and the wall called Betts v. Brady
5:43 Nine to nothing
7:24 The law changed — but not his fate yet
8:48 The right vs. the reality (public defenders)
10:13 A pencil, a letter — a rule for everyone

📚 Sources
Gideon v. Wainwright, 372 U.S. 335 (1963).
Betts v. Brady, 316 U.S. 455 (1942).
Full opinion: https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/106456/gideon-v-wainwright/

Independent educational documentary. Narration is AI-generated. Historical moments that were never filmed are shown as clearly labeled symbolic reconstructions — not authentic footage. This explains how the law works and is not legal advice.
